newsitem.title: USA: Biomaterial suppliers shun U.S. implant market.
newsitem.headline: Biomaterial suppliers shun U.S. implant market.

text.p: Increasing numbers of biomaterial suppliers have banned sales to U.S. implant manufacturers for reasons including the small size of the market and the risk of legal liability, a new study said.
The study by the New York-based Arnoff associates was commissioned by the Health Industry Manufacturers Association (HIMA), which advocates reform of U.S. liability law.

Under current law, suppliers can be brought into litigation even if they were not involved in the design, manufacture or sale of the implant. Courts seldom hold them liable but the lawsuits can still be costly.
"In deciding to sell or not to sell to the implant market, risk of legal liabilty was a key factor for 100 percent of suppliers," said study author Dr. Marvin Aronoff.

"This perceived risk, combined with the small market size for implants -- from 0.002 to three percent of the total market for these materials -- is more than sufficient reason to discourage most suppliers from entering this market, and keeps those companies currently in constantly reviewing whether it makes sense to remain in," he said.

Many implant makers are relying on stockpiled materials, some of which could run out in as little as eight months, the study said. It focused on four materials - PET polyester yarn, polytetrafluoroethylene, polyacetal resin, and molecular weight polyethylene.
Implants include pacemakers, heart valves and catheters.
